title: Graded Nakayama lemma via the irrelevant ideal
description: For an ℕ-graded ring R = ⨁_{i≥0} Rᵢ with irrelevant ideal R₊ = ⨁_{i>0} Rᵢ, and an ℕ-graded module M = ⨁_{n} Mₙ over it, if R₊·M = M then M = 0. Answers the parent entry's second open question: the graded analogue of Nakayama's lemma, with the irrelevant ideal in place of the maximal ideal. Unlike the local-ring forms, the graded statement needs NO finite-generation hypothesis — it follows from a pure bottom-degree argument: if M ≠ 0, take the least degree d carrying a nonzero homogeneous element x; since x ∈ M = R₊·M, its degree-d component is a sum of products Rᵢ·M_{d-i} with i ≥ 1, all of which vanish because M_e = 0 for e < d, contradicting x_d = x ≠ 0. Verified in Lean with 0 axioms and 0 sorries over Mathlib's internal graded-ring / graded-module API.

overview.historicalContext: The graded Nakayama lemma is the workhorse of graded commutative algebra: it is exactly what makes 'a graded module is generated by lifts of a homogeneous basis of M/R₊M' true, and it underlies minimal graded free resolutions, Hilbert-series arguments, and the theory of the Proj of a graded ring. It appears as Lemma 1.4 in Bruns–Herzog and throughout Eisenbud's treatment of graded modules. Where the local Nakayama lemma leans on the determinant trick and the Jacobson radical, the graded version is a one-line degree argument.
overview.problemStatement:
The parent entry nakayama-lemma-oq-01 formalizes the local-ring forms of Nakayama's lemma (𝔪M = M ⟹ M = 0 for finitely generated M). Its second open question asks: does the graded analogue — with the irrelevant ideal R₊ of an ℕ-graded ring in place of 𝔪 — follow, and from what machinery?

**Answer:** Yes, and it is in fact STRONGER: no finite generation is required. The grading itself, via the least nonzero degree, forces M = 0. The 'same Jacobson-radical machinery' suggested by the open question is not needed at all.
overview.text: For an ℕ-graded ring R and an ℕ-graded R-module M, if the irrelevant ideal R₊ satisfies R₊·M = M, then M = 0. The proof needs no finite-generation hypothesis: it uses only the least degree carrying a nonzero homogeneous element, the graded compatibility Rᵢ·Mₑ ⊆ M_{i+e}, and the additive degree-d projection of M. Verified in Lean with 0 axioms.
overview.proofStrategy:
1. projM 𝓜 d : M →+ M — the additive (NOT R-linear) degree-d projection, modelled on Mathlib's GradedRing.proj; it fixes homogeneous elements of degree d and kills those of any other degree.
2. projM_smul_deg — the key vanishing lemma: if every graded piece below degree d is trivial, then for a homogeneous a ∈ Rᵢ of positive degree i ≠ 0 and any n, the degree-d component of a·n vanishes (write n = Σ nₑ; a·nₑ ∈ M_{i+e}, whose degree-d part survives only if i+e = d, forcing e = d−i < d and nₑ = 0).
3. graded_nakayama — assume M ≠ 0. Because M is ℕ-graded, the set of degrees carrying a nonzero homogeneous element is a nonempty subset of ℕ, so it has a least element d (Nat.find); pick 0 ≠ x ∈ M_d. From R₊·M = M, x ∈ R₊·⊤; run Submodule.smul_induction_on with the predicate 'projM d · = 0': the additive step is closed by additivity, and the base step r·n (r ∈ R₊, so its degree-0 component is 0, so every homogeneous piece of r has positive degree) is closed by projM_smul_deg. Hence projM d x = 0; but x is homogeneous of degree d so projM d x = x, giving x = 0, a contradiction.
4. graded_nakayama_top_eq_bot — the submodule restatement ⊤ = ⊥.
keyInsights: **The graded case is FREE of finite generation** — the decisive difference from the local Nakayama lemma. The determinant trick / Jacobson radical are replaced by the well-ordering of ℕ (the module is bounded below by degree 0), so a least nonzero degree exists and the argument is purely combinatorial.

**The degree-d projection is only additive, never R-linear** — and that is exactly why the argument works. R acts by shifting degrees, so projecting onto a fixed degree does NOT commute with the R-action; a faithful graded module must have additive-submonoid graded pieces (not R-submodules), and projM is built as an AddMonoidHom mirroring GradedRing.proj.

**One graded fact does all the shifting**: SetLike.GradedSMul gives Rᵢ·Mₑ ⊆ M_{i+e}. Multiplying by a positive-degree ring element strictly raises degree, so applied to elements supported in degrees ≥ d it lands entirely above d — the mechanism that empties the degree-d component of R₊·M.

**Submodule.smul_induction_on is the clean bridge from the ideal hypothesis to the projection**: proving projM d vanishes on the whole product R₊·⊤ reduces to the single generator step r·n, and there membership r ∈ R₊ is exactly 'degree-0 component of r is zero', which puts every homogeneous piece of r in positive degree.
prerequisites: ℕ-graded rings and modules; the internal-grading picture R = ⨁ Rᵢ, M = ⨁ Mₙ with Rᵢ·Mₑ ⊆ M_{i+e}
The irrelevant ideal R₊ = ⨁_{i>0} Rᵢ and its characterization as {r | degree-0 component is 0}

sections.title: Module Header & Graded Setup
sections.summary: Imports (graded algebra / graded modules / direct-sum decomposition), the module docstring, and the graded typeclass setup. The docstring states the open question inherited from the parent nakayama-lemma-oq-01: the graded analogue of Nakayama, R₊ M = M ⟹ M = 0 for the irrelevant ideal R₊ = ⨁_{i>0} Rᵢ. It explains why the graded case is *both* free of the finite-generation hypothesis and stronger than the local form: instead of the determinant/Jacobson-radical trick, a one-line minimal-degree argument (take the least degree d carrying a nonzero element x; x ∈ R₊ M writes x as a sum of degree-shifted products landing below d, all of which vanish by minimality — contradiction). The variable block fixes an internally ℕ-graded ring 𝒜 : ℕ → σA (GradedRing 𝒜) and an internal graded module 𝓜 : ℕ → σM over it (SetLike.GradedSMul 𝒜 𝓜 with DirectSum.Decomposition 𝓜), with graded pieces as additive submonoids.
sections.mathContext: Graded Nakayama: for $R = \bigoplus_{i\ge0} R_i$ and $M = \bigoplus_n M_n$, if $R_+ M = M$ with $R_+ = \bigoplus_{i>0}R_i$ the irrelevant ideal, then $M = 0$. Uses only $R_i \cdot M_e \subseteq M_{i+e}$ and the least nonzero degree.

sections.title: The additive degree-d projection
sections.summary: projM 𝓜 i : M →+ M, the degree-i component map as an additive homomorphism, modelled on GradedRing.proj. It is deliberately NOT R-linear (the R-action shifts degrees), and projM_apply exposes it as (decompose 𝓜 m i : M).
sections.mathContext: Homogeneous-component projection of a graded module.

sections.title: Key vanishing lemma
sections.summary: projM_smul_deg: if every graded piece below degree d is trivial, then for a homogeneous a ∈ 𝒜 i of positive degree and any n, the degree-d component of a·n is 0. Proved by decomposing n into homogeneous pieces and using Rᵢ·Mₑ ⊆ M_{i+e} to push everything above degree d.

sections.title: Graded Nakayama lemma
sections.summary: graded_nakayama: R₊·M = M ⟹ Subsingleton M. Takes the least degree d carrying a nonzero homogeneous element x, writes x ∈ R₊·⊤, and shows the degree-d projection kills R₊·⊤ via Submodule.smul_induction_on + projM_smul_deg — contradicting projM d x = x ≠ 0.
sections.mathContext: The bottom-degree argument: no finite generation needed.

sections.title: Submodule form
sections.summary: graded_nakayama_top_eq_bot: the restatement (⊤ : Submodule R M) = ⊥ under the same hypothesis.

conclusion.summary: For an ℕ-graded ring R and an ℕ-graded module M, R₊·M = M forces M = 0 — the graded Nakayama lemma. In contrast to the local-ring forms of the parent entry, no finite-generation hypothesis is required: the proof is a pure bottom-degree argument using the least degree carrying a nonzero homogeneous element, the graded compatibility Rᵢ·Mₑ ⊆ M_{i+e}, and the additive degree-d projection. All results are verified with 0 axioms and 0 sorries.
conclusion.implications: Answers the parent entry's second open question and shows the suggested 'Jacobson-radical machinery' is unnecessary — the grading alone suffices, and the finite-generation hypothesis of local Nakayama drops away. This is the lemma behind homogeneous Nakayama lifting (generators of M ↔ generators of M/R₊M) and minimal graded free resolutions.
openQuestions: Derive the graded lifting-of-generators corollary: a set of homogeneous elements of M whose images generate M/R₊M generates M (the graded analogue of the parent's nakayama_span_of_span_quotient), obtained by applying graded_nakayama to the quotient M/⟨lifts⟩.
Extend from ℕ-gradings to ℤ-gradings that are bounded below (Mₙ = 0 for n ≪ 0), where the same least-degree argument applies once boundedness supplies a minimum.

mathlibDependencies.description: The irrelevant ideal R₊ = ⨁_{i>0} Rᵢ of an ℕ-graded ring, characterized by mem_irrelevant_iff as the elements whose degree-0 component vanishes; the graded stand-in for the maximal ideal
Graded compatibility of the module action: a ∈ 𝒜 i, b ∈ 𝓜 j ⟹ a • b ∈ 𝓜 (i + j); the degree-shifting fact that empties the degree-d component of R₊·M
The degree-i component of a homogeneous element of degree i is itself; used to recover x from its degree-d projection
The degree-j component of a homogeneous element of degree i ≠ j is 0; kills off-degree pieces in the vanishing lemma
Induction principle for membership in I • N via single generators r • n and additivity; reduces 'projM d vanishes on R₊·⊤' to the generator step
The additive degree-i projection of a graded ring, the template for the module-level projM built in this file

originalContributions: projM: the degree-i projection of an internal graded module as an additive homomorphism M →+ M (Mathlib provides GradedRing.proj for rings but no module analogue), with projM_apply identifying it as the homogeneous component
projM_smul_deg: the key vanishing lemma — with all graded pieces below degree d trivial, positive-degree ring elements times anything have zero degree-d component
graded_nakayama: the graded Nakayama lemma R₊·M = M ⟹ M = 0 for an ℕ-graded module, with NO finite-generation hypothesis, via the least-nonzero-degree argument
